findings.gate: Charter §4.1 (geography drawable); combat module gate 2; recheck of r1 F-002

draft_evidence.quote: He had stood on the second flight's last step, at the plane's foot, for the whole of it — a minute; he had counted it

comparison_evidence.quote: he had stayed on the third flight, at the plane's foot, beside the man who could not move, with the knife out and the satchel under his arm and his back to Karis against the wall, and had been the reason.

findings.consequence: The r2 repair fixed the number and left the body where it was. 'Two feet' is now consistent (L27, L85, L105), but the chapter places Cael on the third flight three times and on the second flight's last step once, for the same stretch of the same fight, with no movement staged between them: L11 puts him 'on the third flight beside Karis'; L25 has Vastin go 'past Lira and Brom and Karis and Cael on the third flight' on his way up; L55 says he 'had stayed on the third flight, at the plane's foot ... and had been the reason'; L105 says he 'had stood on the second flight's last step, at the plane's foot, for the whole of it'. Both of the last two claim the whole duration and both claim 'at the plane's foot', so they cannot both be true. The geometry does not rescue either: L27 sets the plane's foot at 'the second flight's top step', which is a full flight above the second flight's LAST step, so on the page 'two feet' is asserted at L27 while Cael is still on the third flight and is asserted again at L105 from a step roughly four treads below the plane. This is a chapter that teaches the reader to count flights — the word 'flight' appears twenty-eight times — and then contradicts itself about where its viewpoint character's feet were during the beat the chapter exists to deliver.
findings.repair_target: L11 or L15-L25 — stage the move once, in one clause, when the boxes go down and Vastin goes up (Cael comes up behind him to the second flight's last step, at the plane's foot); then L55 'he had stayed on the third flight' must become the second flight to match L105, and L27's 'the second flight's top step' should be reconciled with 'the second flight's last step' so the plane's foot and Cael's step are the same two feet apart in both descriptions. Do not change the three 'two feet' mentions; they are correct and are the packet's condition.

findings.gate: Craft core — continuity persistence; charter §3.1 (the cataloguing narrator); recheck of r1 F-001

draft_evidence.quote: Three of the four above the plane had come down onto the first flight. The fourth had not. He was on the landing at the cut's head, in the shadow where the stair came down, standing where a man stands who is not going to fight

comparison_evidence.quote: The four at the top came down the first flight at a run and hit the plane as eight hounds had hit it, and did not go over each other, because they were men and men do not; they went into a thing that was not there and stopped as i

findings.consequence: The recount is right in the aggregate and was not carried back one screen. L27 has all four of the top group come down the first flight at a run and strike the plane, hard enough that the narrator notes they 'did not go over each other'; L65 then states that only three came down onto the first flight and that the fourth 'had not' — he was on the landing from the start, 'standing where a man stands who is not going to fight'. Those are not a belief corrected by a later fact, which is what the rewritten L65 is designed to be; they are two incompatible accounts of who ran at the wall. The same carry failure lands again at L79: 'the six of them were six shapes on a landing' is said of a landing holding three men who have just gone back up plus the signaller whose cord one of them cuts — four bodies, not six — and the sentence that follows it, 'a landing in a city has three ways off it and they took all three', is contradicted in the next clause, where the remaining two get up from the steps and leave by the inn's yard gate instead. A reader who accepted the r1 draft's 'four and two' arithmetic is being asked to accept a different arithmetic in three places and the old one in two.
findings.repair_target: L27 — 'The four at the top came down' becomes three, with the crossbow among them (the bolt at L27 must still be spent by one of the three), leaving the fourth on the landing where L65 needs him. L79 — 'the six of them were six shapes on a landing' becomes four, or the sentence widens honestly to cover the two on the steps ('the four on the landing and the two on the steps, and then none of them'), and 'they took all three' is limited to the ones who actually left by the landing. L31 and L55's 'the four above the plane' can stand, since the landing is above the plane, but check them against whatever wording L27 takes.

findings.gate: Charter §3.1 (the cataloguing narrator); craft core reader-trust invariant 1

draft_evidence.quote: was the one he had counted as a stave. He spoke. He said one word up the cut, from the landing, to the crossbow, a word Cael did not catch

comparison_evidence.quote: Six of them. A crossbow above. Staves below. Twenty-two steps, sheer walls, dusk.

findings.consequence: The repaired sentence turns Cael's error from a miscount into a misreading of purpose, which is the right move, but it attributes to him a count he did not make. His catalogue at L11 assigns weapons by end — 'A crossbow above. Staves below.' — and the only description of the top four at L9 is four hoods, one of them with 'a thing at his shoulder that was a crossbow'. No stave is ever counted above the plane. So 'the one he had counted as a stave' asks the reader to check back against a catalogue that says the opposite, in the one paragraph whose entire job is to make the narrator's counting trustworthy. Scope searched: every occurrence of 'stave' and 'staves' in the draft — L9, L11, L43, L47, L51, L53, L65, L79, L81, L93, L97, L127 — and every one of them except the disputed clause at L65 is the two men from the yard gate or their dropped weapons.
findings.repair_target: L65 — 'the one he had counted as a stave' becomes the thing the catalogue actually holds: a hood, a hand, a body, another of the four. 'The one he had counted as a fourth hood' or 'as another pair of hands' both keep the sentence's shape and stop contradicting L11.

concerns: The measure that replaced 'in the length of a breath' at L79 — 'had understood, in the time it takes a man to draw one' — has no antecedent for 'one' in its sentence. The nearest candidate nouns in the list that precedes it are 'a knife in a stave' and 'a boy standing still'; the intended noun is almost certainly a breath, which does not appear. A reader may land on 'draw a knife', which is coherent and even in register, so this is not a proven defect and is not filed as a finding — but on audio the listener has nothing to reach for. Naming the thing drawn costs two words.

Carried over from r1 and untouched by the repair, and now slightly more crowded: Lira is placed on the second flight at L11 and 'came off the second flight's edge onto the man's shoulders from above' at L51, onto a man engaged on the fourth flight — a two-flight drop of roughly eight treads. With Cael's r2 relocation, the second flight now nominally holds Vastin at its top step, Cael at its last step, and Lira at its edge, in a cut a stride and a half wide. Whatever repair F-200 takes should re-check Lira's launching point in the same pass.

The running state file's provisional 'After Chapter 12' row still quotes the r1 notice ('Iron-Wall-adjacent. Vastin. Partial. Iron. Held.') and still describes the team as 'four above with a crossbow; two below with staves; a sixth on the landing' — the seven-body reading the repair removed. This is a state-document lag, not a draft defect, but it will re-inject the old arithmetic into the next packet if it is not updated when Ch12 is spliced.

L73's 'the four had come for it' now sits oddly against the recount: all six came for the cache, and after L65 'the four' is the top group including a man who never came down. The line still reads, since the four above the plane are the ones who were physically over the roof, but if L27 is re-counted per F-201 the phrase is worth a second look in the same pass.

Carried from r1: the packet's opposition includes 'one Anchor course laid across the alley's bottom step — allowed once' and the draft uses none, substituting a spoken signal and Seln's cord. The author declares the deviation and reserves the course for Ch21. The substitution is cleaner dramatically, but it leaves the faceless faction showing no practitioner capability at all in its first appearance inside a city, which is a planning question before Ch21 asks the reader to fear them again.

Carried from r1: paragraph length is very long even for this voice — L79 runs 240 words, L25 228, L47 209 — and the repair added the chapter's longest single sentence at L99. The chapter uses short paragraphs well at its hinges, so the tools are there; a line pass could take one more of them in the middle of exchanges two and four.

Carried from r1: 'he had walked the alley eleven times' (L3) against 'had been right for eight days' (L5). Reconcilable, unfixed by any state document, and deliberately count-shaped, which invites the reader to check it.

Carried from r1, and now the only reason to keep the r1 §5.2 note alive at all: with EXC-B8-CH12-2 recorded, Book 8's prose notice is approved and Book 8 is internally coherent, but B7 Ch13 and the Universe Bible still render the fenced 'FRAGMENT ACQUIRED' block. The series is not coherent with itself. Somebody above this seat should decide whether B7 gets retro-fitted or the divergence is logged as intentional before Book 8 closes.

Carried from r1 and still true: Vastin's Ch10 reflex — the name, the title, the rank — is paid off silently. He holds a wall for a party and never says who he is, and Seln's 'Be nobody' is never quoted at him. The r2 repair left it alone. Keep leaving it alone.
strengths: The repair was surgical. Diffed against r1, exactly eleven paragraphs changed and one was inserted, and every edit sits inside a declared repair target. Nothing was tidied in passing, no paragraph was reordered or merged, and the dialogue block, the four scene breaks and the fixed closing log are byte-identical to the version the r1 seat passed. This is the discipline the craft core asks for in a targeted repair job and it made the recheck cheap.

The new L99 is the best of the repairs and does more than the obligation required. 'Cael entered the limit under it, as a finding and not an aside' puts the faction's ignorance in the narrator's own filing vocabulary rather than in dialogue, sets what they hold against what they do not, and closes on a forward-looking unknown — 'a team that built for a declaration in a cut would build for something else at a line, and he did not know what' — which plants Ch21 without pre-paying a word of it.

L43's added clause fixes two things with one hand. 'for the big one who had righted a cart in a yard where anyone could watch, and for the boy from the report, both of them on the wall's protected side' supplies the motive the two from below never had in r1, pairs Brom with Cael so the card's win-sentence is delivered whole, and does it by reaching back to a scene the reader watched in Ch11 rather than by asserting a reason.

The notice at L111 is now the cleanest fragment record in the book. 'Iron family' removes the tier collision, 'Distinct from the third — Iron-adjacent, the bed; this is not the bed hardened, this is a line drawn on it and kept' names holding against hardening in the log's own register, and the ordinal is checkable against the state file's list of the ten currents, where Iron is third and glossed exactly that way.

The tic repairs replaced a scaffold with instruments rather than with synonyms. 'for a count of three' is a cataloguer's measure, 'for the seconds a charge takes' is a soldier's, and 'while the man's breath came back' is a bedside one; the family that ran five times in r1 now runs zero times, and no replacement is used twice.

The r1 strengths all survived: 'On a road the ground had said go round. Here the ground said there is no round.' (L27); Seln's whole beat with 'Nobody died. Nobody was cut. The signal stopped.' and the cache overhead the whole time (L69-73); Brom standing on the stave instead of hitting a man twice and Lira choosing the shaft over the man (L47, L51); the crew's costs priced in their own vocabulary — 'The sheets are dry', 'Cart was heavier' (L91-95); Vastin asking to be entered in a ledger he no longer keeps (L121); and Cael declining to name the debt on a step (L123).

Mechanical hygiene improved rather than degraded under repair: capped phrases 0, the 'length of a [X]' family 0 (was 5), one-word paragraphs 0, 'the way X [verb]' 2 of 4, forbidden names 0, banned language 0, word count 4,564 and now closer to the 4,600 target than r1's 4,395, and the fixed log still matching the card character for character.
